paragraphs: This paper studies how an electronic neural network’s starting state determines its eventual behavior. Some starting states lead to fixed activity patterns, which serve as memories; others lead to sustained oscillations. The collection of starting states leading to a particular outcome is its basin of attraction.

The researchers built circuitry to map these basins directly. It temporarily disconnects the network’s feedback, sets a starting condition, then observes the attractor reached after feedback resumes. Repeating this process across a systematic grid of initial conditions reveals the shapes of the regions associated with different outcomes.

The measurements show that overloading an associative memory produces irregular memory basins. Adding time delays can also create oscillatory outcomes even when connections are symmetric. The authors relate oscillation to frustration, or competing interaction demands within the network, and show that reducing frustration by removing connections can stabilize a delayed network. These findings connect memory behavior to both connection structure and signal timing.
neurips-1987-basins-of-attraction-for-el.tldr: Electronic measurements show how memory loading, signal delays, and competing connections reshape a neural network’s attraction basins and stability.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a learning rule for nonlinear control that uses repeated visits to nonfailing states as useful feedback. A controller can learn from what happens during an ongoing trial, rather than waiting until a failure reveals that some earlier decisions were unsuccessful.

The method, called recurrence learning, positively reinforces decisions that bring the system back to states where it has avoided failure. The researchers apply it to the BOXES algorithm and the ASE/ACE system. This adds information during exploration to methods whose basic failure-driven updates penalize decisions when a trial ends unsuccessfully.

Simulations show faster learning than both basic failure-driven learning and methods that predict failure. The tested setting is specifically failure-driven control. For tasks with an explicit destination, the authors suggest that recurring cycles could instead deserve negative reinforcement because they may signal unproductive repetition. The broader idea is to interpret recurrence according to the task: returning to a state can provide evidence of safety or evidence that progress has stalled.
neurips-1987-learning-by-state-recurrenc.tldr: Rewarding returns to nonfailing states accelerates learning in the tested control systems by providing feedback before failure occurs.

paragraphs: Recording several neurons at once creates a classification problem: the measured electrical waveforms must be assigned to their sources. Recording one well-isolated neuron at a time simplifies this task, but does not provide the simultaneous view needed to study the activity of many individual neurons together.

The paper compares three approaches to waveform classification. Two formulate template matching through neural networks, while the third uses a simple template-matching implementation. Each approach is designed to identify isolated neural events and separately classify events that overlap in time. Real-time operation is part of the intended task, so the comparison concerns an ongoing recording process.

Analysis using real neural signals favors simple template matching over both neural network formulations. The result matters because overlapping events are a central difficulty in simultaneous recordings, yet introducing a neural network did not provide the better solution in this comparison. The paper therefore contributes both alternative formulations of the classification problem and evidence supporting the simpler approach for the signals studied.
neurips-1987-neural-networks-for-templat.tldr: For classifying real neural waveforms, including overlapping events, simple template matching outperformed two neural network formulations.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether information processing can occur inside the branching structure of a single axon, before signals reach synapses. Its central question concerns signal propagation itself: an axon’s response to incoming activity may shape which signals continue through it, giving transmission a computational role.

The discussion reviews three relevant biological issues: how firing threshold depends on prior activity, when a signal fails to propagate, and how similar different nodes along one axon are. These issues connect the history of stimulation and local axonal properties to the reliability of signal transmission through the same cell.

The paper also presents an electronic model of an axonal location where propagation has a low safety margin. Under stimulation at a single frequency, the circuit behaves as a low-pass filter, preferentially passing lower-frequency activity over higher-frequency activity. This provides a concrete circuit example of the proposed processing role: a vulnerable transmission site can select among temporal inputs. The stated result concerns this circuit model and stimulation condition.
neurips-1987-presynaptic-neural-informat.tldr: An electronic model shows how an axonal site with unreliable conduction can filter activity before it reaches a synapse.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a movement-control architecture that divides the task between generating motor patterns and carrying them out. Its higher stage models the cerebellum as a collection of adjustable pattern generators. Its lower stage consists of local feedback controllers that regulate the forces and lengths of individual muscles.

Sensory information helps prepare and trigger the higher-level generators, and also provides a way to evaluate their performance. Once activated, the generators produce patterned activity through their own internal circuitry. Recurrent loops allow that activity to sustain itself, so the temporal pattern comes from the network’s internal dynamics.

The resulting patterns become feedforward motor commands sent to the local muscle controllers, called motor servos. Those controllers translate the commands into movement through feedback. The architecture therefore assigns different responsibilities to two interacting stages: an adaptive network organizes the motor commands, while local systems regulate their physical execution. Its contribution is a proposed way to combine internally generated movement patterns with sensory evaluation and muscle-level feedback.
neurips-1987-schema-for-motor-control-ut.tldr: A proposed cerebellar controller generates adaptive motor patterns that local muscle feedback systems translate into movement.

paragraphs: This paper extends the Hopfield associative-memory model by allowing each neuron to take more than two values. The question is how to give individual neurons a richer range of responses while retaining the network’s ability to settle into stable states that can represent stored memories.

The authors develop two classes of neuron input-output relationships with convergence guarantees. One class uses continuous relationships; the other specifies permissible quantization rules, which restrict activity to discrete levels. These rules matter because additional neuron values must be accompanied by suitable dynamics if stable memory retrieval is to remain guaranteed.

For networks using the quantized class, the paper reports an information capacity on the order of N cubed bits, where N is the number of neurons. It also develops and investigates an extension of the sum-of-outer-products learning rule. Together, these contributions address how multilevel memories can be encoded, how the network evolves toward stable states, and how stored information scales within the stated class of networks.
neurips-1987-the-hopfield-model-with-mul.tldr: The paper extends Hopfield memory to multilevel neurons, giving convergence rules and an order-N-cubed information capacity for a quantized class.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a learning algorithm for storing both steady patterns and repeating activity cycles in recurrent analog networks. For a network with n nodes, it gives storage of n static attractors or n/2 periodic attractors. A memory can therefore take the form of an ongoing rhythm.

The method separates programming the network’s dynamics from choosing the patterns to store. It allows control over pattern stability, the shapes of attraction basins, and convergence speed. When the patterns are orthonormal, learning simplifies to a periodic version of an outer-product rule, with updates that are local, additive, order-independent, and incremental.

Stored cycles can form standing or traveling waves resembling oscillating spatial activity in olfactory structures. During simulated inspiration, these attractors emerge through a multiple Hopf bifurcation, a transition that creates oscillatory behavior. Near this transition, a very small input can select the resulting attractor. The approach thus links a programmable memory mechanism to the selection of rhythmic patterns in a biologically inspired recognition model.
neurips-1988-a-bifurcation-theory-approa.tldr: A learning algorithm programs stable memories and rhythmic attractors while controlling their dynamics and sensitivity to small selecting inputs.

paragraphs: This paper describes an artificial neuron implemented as a CMOS electronic circuit. The design targets the electrical behavior of neurons over time. Its starting point is a model of voltage-gated channels in the neural membrane, making the biological mechanism the basis for the circuit’s construction.

The connection to a membrane model matters because the intended object of emulation is a neuron’s changing electrical response. Voltage-dependent channel behavior provides the organizing model for that response. The contribution is therefore both a circuit implementation and an approach to translating a biological description into an artificial neuron.

The abstract identifies low power dissipation and a small physical layout as properties of the circuit. These address the authors’ motivation to place more neurons into practical network implementations while pursuing high performance and more accurate emulation. The work brings those concerns together at the level of a single circuit element: the neuron must represent temporal behavior while remaining economical enough in power and space to support denser networks.
neurips-1988-a-low-power-cmos-circuit-wh.tldr: A compact, low-power CMOS neuron derives its design from voltage-gated membrane channels to emulate neuronal electrical behavior over time.

paragraphs: This paper presents a simplified electrical model of the human cochlea’s micromechanics. The authors seek to preserve features they consider essential to its signal processing while expressing the model through electrical elements. The project connects an account of biological hearing with a possible design for acoustic preprocessing.

Simulations show that the model retains four signal-processing features whose importance the authors justify through engineering arguments and evolutionary evidence. The model also uses shared elements to achieve extensive parallel processing with an economical structure. Sharing is central to the approach because the physical organization contributes to how the processing is implemented.

The authors frame the design around five features they regard as essential to the cochlea. Their goals are a useful front-end filter for acoustic images and a clearer understanding of the auditory system. The stated simulation result supports preservation of selected processing properties in the simplified model. Its broader significance is the attempt to make biological organization informative for both an electrical implementation and an explanation of hearing.
neurips-1988-a-passive-shared-element-an.tldr: A simplified electrical cochlea preserves selected signal-processing properties while using shared components for economical parallel processing.

paragraphs: This paper presents a completed design for a fully analog self-organizing feature-map network. Implementing the network requires circuits for both computing activity and adapting connection weights. The authors modify the feature-map algorithm to suit the circuit solutions available for its computations, treating algorithm and hardware design together.

They assess the effects of these modifications by simulating the design as a front end for speech recognition. The design also allows external access to analog weights. That access supports initialization, testing, and static storage, making the learned parameters accessible beyond the circuitry that updates and uses them.

The fully analog implementation requires about one-tenth the area of an earlier comparable digital/analog hybrid version. This makes physical size a major stated advantage of the design. At the reported stage, several components are in fabrication, while the performance assessment comes from simulation. The contribution combines a hardware-adapted learning algorithm, circuits for learning and activation, and a substantial reduction in the area needed for the implementation.
neurips-1988-an-analog-self-organizing-n.tldr: A fully analog feature-map design implements learning and activation in about one-tenth the area of an earlier hybrid version.

paragraphs: This paper addresses how to reconstruct a smooth surface when depth measurements are available only at scattered locations. The proposed solution is an experimental analog VLSI chip that performs interpolation. Its circuit represents a surface-reconstruction model in which depth and slope are coupled to determine the resulting shape.

The network minimizes a second-order energy, described as a thin-plate energy. This gives smoothness a specific role in filling the gaps between observations: the reconstructed surface is selected through the model’s energy objective. Implementing that objective in an analog circuit connects the mathematical formulation directly to a physical computing device.

The researchers designed and successfully tested an eight-node, one-dimensional network using 3-micrometer CMOS technology. That establishes a hardware demonstration at the stated scale. The chip can also produce Gaussian-like image smoothing, linking its interpolation behavior to another visual processing operation. The contribution is a tested circuit realization of the coupled depth-and-slope model, with both sparse-depth interpolation and smoothing as stated capabilities.
neurips-1988-an-analog-vlsi-chip-for-thi.tldr: A tested eight-node analog chip reconstructs smooth depth profiles by minimizing thin-plate energy and can also provide image smoothing.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how multilayer perceptrons trained with backpropagation can classify speech sounds. Its experiments focus on recognizing 16 American English vowels independently of the speaker. The authors use this task to study how network design and training choices affect phonetic classification, reporting results comparable to human performance.

The investigation includes combining heterogeneous information sources, examining learned internal representations, comparing error measures, and choosing initial network settings. It also compares the network with K-nearest-neighbor and Gaussian classifiers. Classification improves as more information becomes available, and the authors describe implementation choices that improve performance and make learning more efficient.

The broader motivation is to connect speech knowledge with a trainable classification procedure. Linguistic and acoustic knowledge can guide the network’s structure, while learning supplies a way to use that knowledge in decisions. The paper therefore treats recognition accuracy and representation design as related questions: what information enters the model, how training organizes it, and which choices allow it to support reliable distinctions between vowels.
neurips-1988-applications-of-error-back-.tldr: Backpropagation networks achieve human-comparable results on speaker-independent vowel classification while revealing how information and training choices affect recognition.

paragraphs: This paper presents ALVIS, a neural architecture that learns associations in continuous environments with multiple dimensions. Reinforcement identifies locations associated with favorable or unfavorable outcomes. The system stores these discoveries separately, creating representations of places to approach and places to avoid as it learns about its environment.

For the current goal, ALVIS combines the outputs of the relevant positive and negative subnetworks. It compares that combined information with its present location to produce an error vector. This vector expresses a direction of desired change in the represented environment, incorporating both attraction toward favorable locations and avoidance of unfavorable ones.

The system then backpropagates the error through a network that maps between motor actions and perceptions. This produces an action vector intended to move it in the desired direction. A simulated robot performing a target-seeking task demonstrates the architecture. The key contribution is a complete path from reinforcement memories to action: learned preferences over locations become movement guidance through the motor-perceptual mapping.
neurips-1988-associative-learning-via-in.tldr: ALVIS turns learned memories of favorable and unfavorable locations into actions that guide a simulated robot toward a target.

paragraphs: This paper examines how backpropagation can be encouraged to construct simpler networks while learning a task. It builds on a proposal to add penalty terms to the usual training error. Those penalties bias the search toward simpler representations and can help determine how many hidden units are needed.

The authors compare two such biases on simple counting tasks and a speech recognition problem. The underlying aim is to let training shape both the solution and its internal representation. A network that needs fewer hidden units may express the problem more compactly, which motivates the proposed connection to improved generalization.

The reported result is that constrained search generally appears to reduce the number of hidden units required. It also brings an expected increase in local minima, creating more opportunities for training to settle into locally favorable solutions. The comparison therefore identifies a tradeoff within the learning objective: encouraging simplicity can produce smaller representations while making the search for a satisfactory set of weights more difficult.
neurips-1988-comparing-biases-for-minima.tldr: Penalties favoring simpler networks reduce required hidden units in the reported tasks but increase the prevalence of local minima.

paragraphs: This paper applies parallelizable optimization methods to learning in feedforward neural networks. The central concern is the procedure used to find suitable connection weights. By changing that procedure, the authors seek more efficient training and better convergence while keeping feedforward-network learning as the underlying problem.

The methods include Polak–Ribiere optimization, which the paper compares with the backpropagation algorithm. The experiments cover small Boolean learning problems and handwritten character recognition with noisy, real-valued data. These tasks place the comparison in both discrete problems and a recognition setting with inputs that vary continuously and contain noise.

The reported findings favor the optimization techniques in both convergence behavior and efficiency. This suggests that the choice of weight-search method can materially affect how readily a network learns, beyond the choice of network itself. Parallelizability is also part of the proposed approach, making the organization of computation relevant to the training method. The evidence stated in the abstract concerns the Boolean and handwritten-character tasks used in the experiments.
neurips-1988-efficient-parallel-learning.tldr: Parallelizable optimization methods, including Polak–Ribiere, improve training efficiency and convergence over backpropagation in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: This paper explores a neural controller whose elements and connection patterns are deliberately heterogeneous. The motivation comes from animal nervous systems, where diverse components support flexible behavior in changing environments. The authors apply that idea to controlling a simulated insect’s walking, drawing on biological studies of insect locomotion.

The controller produces a variety of statically stable gaits at different speeds. These changes can be obtained simply by varying the sustained activity of one cell. A single control signal therefore influences the coordinated behavior of the larger network, allowing different walking patterns to arise from the same architecture.

The simulated controller also adapts to perturbations as a consequence of its design. This links the organization of the network to both gait generation and responses to disturbance. The paper’s contribution is a concrete example of how differences among neural elements and their connections can support behavioral flexibility. Its stated findings concern the simulated insect, where the designed interactions produce multiple stable walking patterns and adaptive responses.
neurips-1988-heterogeneous-neural-networ.tldr: A heterogeneous neural controller gives a simulated insect multiple stable gaits and adaptive responses to disturbances.

paragraphs: This paper investigates a connection between two approaches to speech recognition. Hidden Markov models naturally represent sequences and can be trained statistically, but the authors identify limited flexibility from a predetermined topology and weak discrimination. Multilayer perceptrons offer classification capabilities, while the sequential structure of speech is harder for them to handle.

The authors define a discriminant hidden Markov model and then relate it to a particular multilayer perceptron. That perceptron includes contextual input units and additional feedback inputs. These additions are central to the relationship because they extend the information available to the classifier beyond an isolated input pattern.

The paper shows that this specially structured perceptron can be interpreted as a general form of the discriminant Markov model. This is a representational result connecting sequence modeling and classification within a common framework. It matters because the two approaches address complementary aspects of speech: the ordering of information through time and the ability to distinguish among candidate classes. The proposed link makes their relationship explicit.
neurips-1988-links-between-markov-models.tldr: A perceptron with contextual and feedback inputs is shown to generalize a discriminant hidden Markov model.

paragraphs: This paper uses analog VLSI circuitry to model central pattern generators, small biological networks that produce rhythms for locomotion. The focus is on reproducing the ongoing patterns generated by interacting neurons. Such a model must capture how activity develops over time and how circuit interactions sustain a rhythm.

The researchers design, fabricate, and test a neuron circuit that uses mechanisms also found in biological pattern-generator neurons, including delays and internal feedback. These mechanisms make timing and recurrent influence part of the circuit’s operation. The resulting neuron is then used as a building block for several small network configurations.

Those configurations are based on known biological central pattern generators, and their outputs closely resemble the observed biological activity patterns. The result connects the design of individual electronic neurons to the rhythms produced by assembled networks. The contribution is therefore a tested hardware modeling approach: biologically motivated temporal mechanisms at the neuron level can support recognizable biological patterns when the circuits are connected into small networks.
neurips-1988-modeling-small-oscillating-.tldr: Fabricated analog neuron circuits use delays and feedback to reproduce activity patterns resembling biological locomotion rhythm generators.

paragraphs: This paper models the mammalian olfactory bulb using its anatomy and electrical activity as guides. The aim is to explain how odor input becomes output sent toward olfactory cortex. In the model, odor-related decision states can be stable repeating cycles, giving ongoing activity a direct role in representing information.

Simulations produce coordinated, modulated activity across the bulb at 35–60 Hz, resembling observed field potentials. Analysis and simulation attribute these rhythms to coupled nonlinear oscillators whose activity depends on the odor input. The model therefore connects the temporal pattern of neural activity with the information being processed.

The work also shows that appropriate signals from higher centers can increase or decrease sensitivity to particular odors. This places odor processing within an interacting system in which incoming sensory information and higher-level inputs jointly shape the response. The contribution is a mathematical framework linking odor-dependent rhythms, coordinated bulb activity, and adjustable sensitivity to the transformation from sensory input to cortical output.
neurips-1988-modeling-the-olfactory-bulb.tldr: Coupled nonlinear oscillators model odor-dependent bulb rhythms and show how higher-center inputs can adjust sensitivity to particular odors.

paragraphs: This paper applies a neural network to distinguishing similar handwritten Kanji characters. The task centers on characters whose visual resemblance makes classification demanding. The researchers train a three-layer feedforward network with backpropagation and introduce two additional methods intended to make the training process effective.

The trained network achieves higher recognition accuracy than the conventional methods used in the comparison. The authors also analyze its connection weights to investigate how it reaches its decisions. That analysis indicates that the network can distinguish the hierarchical structure of Kanji characters, linking recognition behavior to the organization of the written forms.

The paper attributes the strong recognition results to this learned strategy. Its contribution therefore includes both a character classifier and an interpretation of the representation supporting its performance. Training appears to make structural distinctions useful to the network, helping it separate characters that look similar. The stated findings support neural networks as an effective approach to the Kanji recognition problem examined in the study.
neurips-1988-neural-networks-that-learn-.tldr: A backpropagation network distinguishes similar handwritten Kanji with improved accuracy and learns representations reflecting their hierarchical structure.

paragraphs: This paper describes integrated circuits for asynchronous analog neural networks in which neurons communicate through streams of pulses. The implementation must represent connection strengths and apply them to signals traveling between neurons. It does this using dynamically stored synaptic weights and a time-division mechanism for weighting the pulses.

The central circuit idea uses MOS transistors in their conducting state as variable resistors. These resistors control the discharge of a capacitor, providing the electrical mechanism for time division. Through this arrangement, a small synapse circuit cell controls how the pulse signal from a sending neuron influences a receiving neuron.

The chip-set design uses 2.5-micrometer CMOS technology. Its contribution is a concrete hardware organization joining pulse-based communication, analog operation, and programmable connection strengths. The small synapse cell is especially relevant because it provides the weighting function at the point where neurons connect. The paper thus explains how timing and capacitor discharge can implement synaptic weighting within an integrated asynchronous neural-network design.
neurips-1988-programmable-analog-pulse-f.tldr: An asynchronous analog chip design weights neural pulse streams through compact synapse circuits that control capacitor-discharge timing.

paragraphs: This paper proposes skeletonization, a method for simplifying a neural network by assessing how much its individual units matter. The guiding idea is to use what the trained network has learned to identify which inputs and hidden units are critical to its performance and which contribute redundant information.

The procedure repeats a sequence: train to a specified performance level, calculate a relevance measure, and remove the least relevant units. This makes simplification depend on the network’s learned function. Both input units and hidden units can be considered, so the process can reduce the information supplied to the network as well as its internal machinery.

The authors describe three uses for this approach: eliminating redundancy, improving learning by starting with spare hidden units and later removing unnecessary ones, and interpreting behavior through a smaller set of rules. Trimming also constrains generalization by reducing the retained representation. The contribution ties network size and interpretability to an explicit assessment of functional relevance after learning.
neurips-1988-skeletonization-a-technique.tldr: Skeletonization repeatedly trains a network and removes its least relevant units to simplify representations and expose their essential structure.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a neural network and learning algorithm for producing accurate, smoothly varying outputs from analog data. The architecture has input, hidden, output, and final-output stages, with multiple hidden and output layers. The learning procedure is called SICL, short for Spread Pattern Information and Cooperative Learning.

The stated purpose of SICL is to combine accurate learning of analog values with smooth output behavior. These are complementary requirements for the proposed speech-production application: the system must generate the desired values while also producing outputs that vary smoothly. The network architecture and cooperative learning mechanism are presented together as the means of achieving this.

The authors build a speech-production system with two subsystems, one producing phonemic symbols and the other producing speech parameters. They report successfully generating natural speech waveforms with high accuracy. The contribution therefore spans a proposed learning mechanism and its use in a complete speech-production arrangement, connecting the network’s analog-output properties to the resulting speech signals.
neurips-1988-speech-production-using-a-n.tldr: A cooperative-learning network produces smooth analog outputs and is used in a system reported to generate accurate, natural speech waveforms.

paragraphs: This paper addresses the computational complexity of stochastic Boltzmann machines. Their appeal for classification comes from the relationship between network energy and the probability of reaching particular states. That relationship allows probabilities of different outcomes to be associated with decisions, but the authors regard stochastic operation as a practical obstacle.

They propose converting a Boltzmann machine into a deterministic feedforward model called the Boltzmann Perceptron Network. The resulting network is described as functionally equivalent while having lower complexity and requiring no annealing. The paper gives conditions under which the conversion is possible, so the equivalence is tied to those conditions.

The authors also provide a learning algorithm based on conjugate gradients that resembles backpropagation. The contribution combines a change in computational structure with a way to train the resulting model. It aims to retain the decision-making function associated with the Boltzmann machine while expressing that function through a deterministic forward computation, reducing the operational burden identified in the stochastic formulation.
neurips-1988-the-boltzmann-perceptron-ne.tldr: Under stated conversion conditions, a deterministic feedforward network reproduces a Boltzmann machine’s function without annealing.

paragraphs: This paper asks how much training data a neural network needs before good training performance supports confidence in future predictions. It assumes random training examples and future test examples come from the same probability distribution. The analysis relates the amount of data to network size and the desired prediction accuracy.

For feedforward networks of linear-threshold units, the authors give sufficient sample-size bounds involving the numbers of nodes and weights. With enough random examples and sufficiently accurate classification of those examples, the result provides high confidence that the network will classify the required fraction of future examples correctly.

The paper also establishes a complementary lower-bound result for fully connected networks with one hidden layer. With too few training examples, any learning algorithm can fail with a fixed nonzero frequency on some distributions, even when suitable weights exist. Together, the results distinguish sufficient evidence for generalization from unavoidable data requirements. The guarantee depends on the shared training-and-test distribution assumption and the network classes addressed by the analysis.
neurips-1988-what-size-net-gives-valid-g.tldr: The paper bounds how training-set size must relate to network size for reliable generalization under a shared training-and-test distribution.
